hook.situation: You are reacting in real time: Korean feels more fun than expected, someone has already arrived, a friend may be late, and a missed plan still feels disappointing. The grammar is in the ending because the ending tells the listener how you are taking the information.
objectives: Use -네요 for fresh realization from what you just noticed.
Use -군요/-구나 for stronger acknowledgement or exclamation.
Use -(으)ㄹ걸요 for a softened prediction and -았/었을 텐데요 for regret or unfulfilled expectation.
hook.whyItMatters: A plain statement reports information. These endings report your stance toward the information. 재미있어요, 재미있네요, and 재미있군요 can describe the same fact, but they do not sound like the same reaction.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-네요: realizing or noticing something right now
grammarNotes.func: -네요 is the on-the-spot reaction ending. You attach it when you discover, see, hear, taste, or otherwise newly notice something at the moment of speaking. It carries a light feeling of mild surprise or fresh awareness: "Oh, it's ...!" Use it when the information just hit you, not when you are reporting a fact you already knew.

examples.en: Oh, it's raining outside.
examples.note: You just looked out and noticed the rain now -- that fresh discovery is exactly what -네요 marks.

examples.en: Wow, this kimchi stew is really delicious!
examples.note: Said after the first bite -- a reaction to something you are experiencing at this moment.

examples.en: It's already 6. Time flies.
examples.note: Noticing the clock and the speed of time on the spot; 빠르네요 reacts to a realization, not a stored fact.

examples.en: You really speak Korean well!
examples.note: A natural compliment -- you just heard them speak and are reacting, which is why -네요 sounds warm here.

keyPoint.label: -네요 = reacting to NEW information
keyPoint.body: The core trigger is newness to the speaker. If you already knew the fact and are just stating it, use plain -아/어요. The moment of fresh noticing is what makes -네요 the right choice.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: Past tense -았네요/-었네요 has the ㅅ assimilate to ㄴ: 끝났네요 sounds like [끈난네요], 갔네요 like [간네요]. Learners who pronounce a clear [ㅅ] here sound non-native.

drill.instruction: React in the moment using A/V-네요. Fill in the blank with the verb/adjective in parentheses.
items: 여기 사람이 많이 (있다) -> 여기 사람이 많이 ____.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 어제 비가 왔네요. (to report yesterday's weather you already knew)
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 어제 비가 왔어요. / (noticing puddles now) 비가 왔네요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers reach for -네요 whenever something feels noteworthy, but it must mark information that is new to you at the moment of speaking. Reporting a fact you already knew takes plain -아/어요; -네요 only fits when you are noticing it fresh.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-군요 / -구나: "I see, so that's how it is"
grammarNotes.func: -군요 (polite) and -구나 (casual) express the moment of understanding: you take in new information and acknowledge it, often realizing the reason or background behind something. Where -네요 is a gut reaction to what you perceive, -군요/-구나 is the click of comprehension -- "Ah, so THAT'S why / so it's like that."

formTable.ex: 가다 -> 가는군요 / 가는구나 (I see, you're going)
아프다 -> 아팠군요 / 아팠구나 (Ah, you were sick)
동생이군요 / 동생이구나 (Oh, it's your younger sibling)

examples.en: Ah, so that's why you couldn't come yesterday.
examples.note: 그래서 + -군요 is the classic pairing: you just grasped the reason behind something.

examples.en: So THIS is that famous restaurant.
examples.note: You connect what you heard before with what you now see -- a moment of recognition, not just surprise.

examples.en: I see, so Minsu is good at cooking.
examples.note: Verb 잘하다 takes -는군요 in the present; you are registering a newly learned fact about Minsu.

examples.en: Oh, you already graduated. Time really flies.
examples.note: Casual -구나 to a close friend; it shows you absorbing news and reflecting on it.

keyPoint.label: Verbs need -는군요 in the present
keyPoint.body: Adjectives and nouns attach -군요 directly (춥군요, 학생이군요), but present-tense verbs insert -는-: 가는군요, 먹는군요. Past tense is uniform for both: -았/었군요. -구나 is simply the casual (반말) version.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: -는군요 links the final ㄴ into the 요 in fast speech, sounding like [는군뇨]. The casual -구나 is often drawn out for feeling: 그렇구나~, signaling a thoughtful "ahh, I see."

drill.instruction: Show that you just understood something using -군요 (polite) or -구나 (casual).
items: (그래서 전화를 안 받았다) -> 그래서 전화를 안 ____.
(이 노래를 직접 만들었다) -> 이 노래를 직접 ____.
(casual: 너도 이 영화 봤다) -> 너도 이 영화 ____.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers attach -군요 straight to every stem because adjectives work that way (춥군요). But present-tense verbs require the inserted -는-: 잘하다 -> 잘하는군요, 먹다 -> 먹는군요. Forgetting -는- is the single most common mistake with this ending.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-(으)ㄹ걸요: "probably," a soft guess
grammarNotes.func: -(으)ㄹ걸요 offers a tentative guess based on your own reasoning or hunch, softened so it doesn't sound too sure. It means "I think probably ..." or "it's likely that ...," and is common when answering someone gently without claiming certainty. (Written the same, -(으)ㄹ걸 그랬다 with a sighing tone means regret, "I should have ...," but here we focus on the guessing use.)

examples.en: The shop is probably closed now.
examples.note: A soft prediction about a present situation; -았을걸요 guesses the door is already in a closed state.

examples.ko: 민지 씨는 매운 거 잘 먹을걸요.
examples.romanization: minji ssineun maeun geo jal meogeulgeoryo.
examples.en: Minji can probably handle spicy food well.
examples.note: You're guessing from what you know of her -- not stating a fact, just a confident-but-soft hunch.

examples.en: That movie has probably already ended.
examples.note: Past-guess -았을걸요 estimates about something completed; very natural in casual conversation.

examples.en: Since it's the weekend, the roads will probably be jammed.
examples.note: Reasoning from a known cause (주말이라서) to a likely outcome -- the textbook use of a soft guess.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄹ걸요 = your guess, not shared knowledge
keyPoint.body: Use -(으)ㄹ걸요 when the conclusion comes from your own inference and you want to stay humble about it. Compare -(으)ㄹ 거예요, which sounds more confident/declarative. -걸요 always softens, as if to say "I'm fairly sure, but don't quote me."

grammarNotes.pronunciation: The 걸 is tensed to [껄]: 올걸요 sounds like [올껄요], 먹을걸요 like [머글껄요]. The sentence also rises slightly at the end, giving it its tentative, musing feel.

drill.instruction: Answer with a soft guess using V/A-(으)ㄹ걸요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 내일 비가 올 거예요. (when you only have a vague hunch, not real evidence)
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 내일 비가 올걸요. (a soft, unsure guess) -- use 올 거예요 only when you're genuinely confident.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English "probably" and "will" feel interchangeable, so learners default to -(으)ㄹ 거예요 even for hunches. But -(으)ㄹ 거예요 sounds like a confident claim, while -(으)ㄹ걸요 keeps it hedged. Match the ending to how sure you actually are. Also keep -(으)ㄹ걸요 (guess) separate from -(으)ㄹ걸 그랬다 (regret, "I should have").

grammarNotes.title: V-았/었을 텐데(요): "it would have ..., but"
grammarNotes.func: -았/었을 텐데(요) expresses a confident guess about an unrealized past -- what surely would have happened -- usually paired with a contrasting reality, regret, or concern. It looks back and supposes: "It would have been ... (but it wasn't / but something got in the way)." The 텐데 leaves the thought hanging, inviting sympathy or a soft follow-up rather than a blunt complaint.

formTable.ex: 오다 -> 왔을 텐데요 (They would have come)
시간이 있었으면 갔을 텐데요 (If I'd had time, I'd have gone)
쉽다 -> 쉬웠을 텐데요 (It would have been easy)
바쁘다 -> 바쁠 텐데요 (They must be busy, though)

examples.ko: 어제 시간이 있었으면 같이 갔을 텐데요.
examples.romanization: eoje sigani isseosseumyeon gachi gasseul tendeyo.
examples.en: If I'd had time yesterday, I would have gone with you.
examples.note: The trip didn't happen; -았/었을 텐데요 keeps the regret soft instead of stating a flat "I couldn't go."

examples.en: If I'd known in advance, I would have helped.
examples.note: Polite regret after missing a chance to help -- 미리 알았으면 sets the unreal condition.

examples.ko: 조금만 일찍 왔으면 표를 살 수 있었을 텐데요.
examples.romanization: jogeumman iljjik wasseumyeon pyoreul sal su isseosseul tendeyo.
examples.en: If you'd come just a bit earlier, you could have bought a ticket.
examples.note: Gentle 'too bad' about a missed chance; the 텐데 trails off, softening it.

examples.en: If you'd taken the bus, you wouldn't have been late.
examples.note: Looking back at what would have avoided the problem -- sympathetic, not accusatory.

keyPoint.label: Past -았/었을 텐데 = unreal past; present -(으)ㄹ 텐데 = current concern
keyPoint.body: Add the past -았/었- when you're supposing about something that did NOT happen (regret): 갔을 텐데요. Drop it for a present/future worry or contrast: 지금 바쁠 텐데요 ("they must be busy right now, though"). Mixing these changes the meaning from regret to ongoing concern.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 텐데 is [텐데] with a clear, even tone, but the sentence-final 요 trails off and drops in pitch -- that falling, unfinished melody is what signals the lingering 'but...' feeling. Don't end it sharply.

drill.instruction: Express soft regret about an unreal past using -았/었으면 ... -았/었을 텐데요.
drill.model: (시간 / 같이 가다) -> 시간이 있었으면 같이 갔을 텐데요.
items: (연습 많이 하다 / 쉽다) -> 연습을 많이 했으면 훨씬 ____.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 시간이 있으면 같이 갔을 텐데요. (present 있으면 with a past-regret result)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: For regret about the past, the IF-clause must also be past-unreal: 있었으면, not 있으면. English "if I had time" hides the tense, so learners use present 있으면 and clash with the past 갔을 텐데요. Match both halves to the unreal past: 있었으면 ... 갔을 텐데요.

grammarNotes.title: -군요 vs -네요: both react, but not the same way
grammarNotes.func: -네요 and -군요 both respond to new information, but with a different feel. -네요 is an immediate, conversational gut reaction to what you directly perceive right now ("oh, look at that"). -군요 is a slightly more composed acknowledgement -- you take in a fact or explanation and register it ("I see, so that's the case"). Knowing which one to reach for keeps your reactions sounding natural.

formTable.when: Acknowledging a fact/explanation you just learned

formTable.ex: 그래서 못 왔군요 (So that's why you couldn't come)

examples.en: Oh, it's snowing!
examples.note: -네요: a spontaneous reaction to what you see out the window this second.

examples.en: Ah, so that's why you were late.
examples.note: -군요: you take in the explanation and acknowledge the reason -- calmer than a gut reaction.

examples.en: I see. I had it wrong.
examples.note: Both in one breath: 군요 accepts the new fact, 네요 marks your own fresh realization about yourself.

examples.en: The coffee here is really good.
examples.note: -네요: a direct, in-the-moment reaction to taste -- 맛있군요 would sound oddly stiff here.

keyPoint.label: Perceiving now -> -네요; registering a fact -> -군요
keyPoint.body: If you're reacting to something you directly sense at this moment (taste, weather, someone's arrival), -네요 sounds warm and natural. If you're acknowledging information or a reason that just clicked, -군요 fits. -군요 can sound stiff for simple sensory reactions, and -네요 can sound under-reactive for absorbing a full explanation.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 그렇군요 is pronounced [그러쿠뇨] (ㅎ + ㄱ tenses/aspirates to ㅋ), and 그렇네요 is [그런네요] (ㅎ assimilates to ㄴ before ㄴ). Both are extremely common backchannels -- saying them clearly helps you sound like an engaged listener.

drill.instruction: Choose -네요 (direct noticing) or -군요 (acknowledging a fact/reason), then fill the blank.
drill.model: (친구 설명을 듣고) 아, 그래서 그랬____. -> 그랬군요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: For a direct, in-the-moment sensory reaction (taste, weather, a view), Korean prefers -네요; -군요 sounds too composed or bookish there. Learners over-use -군요 because it's taught as "I see," but reserve it for acknowledging facts or reasons, not for spontaneous "wow, this is good!" reactions.

exampleSentence.en: Korean is more fun than I expected.
It is not as hard as I thought.
exampleSentence.note: This word naturally triggers realization endings because expectation changed.

exampleSentence.ko: 처음에는 어려울 줄 알았는데 생각보다 괜찮군요.
exampleSentence.en: I thought it would be hard at first, but it is better than expected.
exampleSentence.note: 어려울 줄 알았다 sets the old expectation.
벌써 pairs well with surprise or realization.
Past honorific 도착하셨군요 fits polite acknowledgement.

exampleSentence.en: If you leave now, you will probably be a little late.
If I had had time, I would have gone with you.
exampleSentence.note: 시간이 있었으면 creates the missed condition.

exampleSentence.en: I would have gone together with you.
exampleSentence.note: 같이 makes the regret relational, not just logistical.
이미 often appears in hedged assertions.

exampleSentence.en: There are more people than expected.
It probably is not certain yet.
If I had said it clearly, there would have been no misunderstanding.
exampleSentence.note: 분명히 sharpens the missed action in a regret sentence.

extendedVocabulary.nuance: 분명히 has two jobs: it can describe saying something clearly (분명히 말하다) or strengthen certainty (‘definitely’). In the certainty use it overlaps heavily with 확실히, so context and collocation are more reliable than a rigid subjective-versus-objective split.

extendedVocabulary.english: to be natural, obvious, no wonder

exampleSentence.ko: 연습을 많이 했으니까 잘하는 게 당연하네요.
exampleSentence.en: Since you practiced a lot, no wonder you are good.
exampleSentence.note: -네요 makes the comment a realization, not a dismissive judgment.

exampleSentence.en: That must have been really hard for you.
exampleSentence.note: -군요 can acknowledge someone else's experience with empathy.
알고 있을걸요 is a common hedged assertion.

extendedVocabulary.nuance: For a neutral ‘I don't know,’ Korean normally uses 모르다: 몰라요 or the softer 잘 모르겠어요. 안 알아요 is not universally wrong; context can give it ‘I don't recognize/know,’ ‘I won't find out,’ or a contrastive denial, so do not treat it as an impossible form.

exampleSentence.en: I see. I did not know that.
exampleSentence.note: 군요 accepts the fact; 네요 marks the speaker's realization.

extendedDialogue.setting: Friends react to a class, a late schedule, and a missed chance while choosing endings that match their stance.

lines.romanization: cheoeumeneun eoryeoul jul aranneunde saenggakboda gwaenchanhgunyo.

lines.speaker: 민서

lines.grammarNote: -네요 works because Minseo is noticing the arrival.

lines.speaker: 지훈

lines.speaker: 민서

lines.romanization: eoje sigani isseosseumyeon gachi gasseul tendeyo.
lines.en: If I had had time yesterday, I would have gone with you.
lines.grammarNote: -았/었을 텐데요 carries regret for an unreal past.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 연습을 많이 했으니까 잘하는 게 당연하네요.
lines.romanization: yeonseubeul mani haesseunikka jalhaneun ge dangyeonhaneyo.
lines.en: Since you practiced a lot, no wonder you are good.
lines.grammarNote: 당연하네요 explains a realization without sounding blunt.

readingText.title: 끝 어미가 태도를 바꾼다
readingText.body: 민서는 첫 수업을 듣고 "생각보다 재미있네요"라고 말했다. 방금 느낀 놀라움이라서 -네요가 자연스러웠다. 지훈은 설명을 듣고 "그렇군요"라고 했다. 새 정보를 받아들이는 조금 더 차분한 반응이었다. 수업이 끝난 뒤 선생님이 이미 도착한 것을 보고 민서는 "벌써 도착하셨네요"라고 했고, 지훈은 시간을 보더니 "지금 출발하면 늦을걸요"라고 했다. 나중에 민서는 약속에 가지 못한 일을 떠올리며 "시간이 있었으면 같이 갔을 텐데요"라고 말했다. 같은 사실도 끝 어미가 달라지면 놀람, 인정, 예측, 아쉬움이 서로 다르게 들린다.
readingText.bodyTranslation: After the first class, Minseo said, "It is more fun than I expected." Because it was a surprise she had just felt, -네요 was natural. Jihoon listened to an explanation and said, "I see." That was a calmer acknowledgement of new information. After class, Minseo saw that the teacher had already arrived and said, "Oh, the teacher has already arrived." Jihoon looked at the time and said, "If we leave now, we will probably be late." Later, Minseo remembered not being able to go to an appointment and said, "If I had had time, I would have gone with you." Even with the same facts, the final ending changes whether the sentence sounds like surprise, acknowledgement, prediction, or regret.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 첫 수업 뒤에 어떤 어미를 사용했어요?
지훈이 "늦을걸요"라고 한 이유는 무엇이에요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 지금 출발하면 늦을 것 같다고 부드럽게 예측했기 때문이에요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: -았/었을 텐데요는 어떤 느낌을 나타냈어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 과거에 이루어지지 않은 일에 대한 아쉬움이나 후회를 나타냈어요.

culturalNote.title: 끝 어미는 목소리의 표정
culturalNote.body: In Korean, the final ending often carries the social expression that English might put in intonation. 재미있어요 reports a fact. 재미있네요 shares a fresh reaction. 재미있군요 sounds like a more formal acknowledgement. 늦을걸요 warns softly without sounding bossy. 갔을 텐데요 lets regret trail off instead of making a heavy complaint.
culturalNote.tip: Before choosing the ending, ask: am I noticing, acknowledging, guessing, or regretting?

inlineExercises.prompt: Which ending fits a fresh realization after trying Korean class?
Which sentence is a softened prediction?
inlineExercises.explanation: -ㄹ걸요 gives a hedged assertion or prediction.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence expresses regret about a missed past condition?
Complete the acknowledgement: 아, 그런 이유였____. (use -군요)
inlineExercises.explanation: 그런 이유였군요 politely acknowledges a newly understood reason.

inlineExercises.prompt: 생각___ 더 재미있네요. (It is more fun than I expected.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 생각보다 means compared with what I thought or expected. -네요 then reacts to the fresh realization.
-네요 marks something you notice now. 어렵다 becomes 어렵네요.
-군요 acknowledges or takes in information with a stronger “I see” feeling. 벌써 adds the surprise that it already happened.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the regret: '같이 갔으면 좋겠어요.' (missed past plan)
inlineExercises.explanation: For regret about a missed past plan, the result needs past hypothetical language. 좋았을 텐데요 expresses the unfulfilled expectation.

inlineExercises.prompt: You just tried the class and are surprised it is fun. Which fits?
inlineExercises.explanation: -네요 fits fresh realization from direct experience. -ㄹ걸요 is a guess, and -었을 텐데요 is regret/hypothetical.

inlineExercises.prompt: Complete the soft guess: 지금 출발하면 아마 안 늦___. (use -(으)ㄹ걸요)
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ걸요 gives a soft, unconfirmed guess. 늦다 ends in the consonant ㅈ, so it takes 을걸요: 안 늦을걸요.

bullets: -네요 marks a fresh realization: 생각보다 재미있네요, 벌써 도착하셨네요.
-군요/-구나 marks stronger acknowledgement or exclamation: 그렇군요, 알고 있었구나.
-(으)ㄹ걸요 softens a prediction or assertion: 늦을걸요, 이미 알고 있을걸요.
-았/었을 텐데요 looks back at an unfulfilled past expectation: 같이 갔을 텐데요.

writingTask.prompt: A friend just arrived and you notice the time. Send a 3-line reaction: react to something you just noticed, show you now understand why, and add a soft guess.
writingTask.hint: Use A/V-네요 for an on-the-spot reaction, A/V-군요 for 'I see,' and -(으)ㄹ걸요 for a soft guess.
writingTask.model: 벌써 도착했네요! 길이 안 막혔군요. 지금 가면 안 늦을걸요.
writingTask.modelEn: Oh, you've arrived already! I see, the road wasn't jammed. If we go now, we probably won't be late.

canDo: React to something noticed right now with A/V-네요 (벌써 도착했네요)
Acknowledge newly understood information with A/V-군요 / -구나 (안 막혔군요)
Offer a soft, reasoned guess with V/A-(으)ㄹ걸요 (안 늦을걸요)
Suppose about an unrealized past with V-았/었을 텐데(요) (늦었을 텐데요)
